Chapter Six: The Courage to See — Facing Our Own Self-Deception.
Have you ever felt that quiet, uneasy feeling when you start to wonder if maybe—just maybe—you're part of the problem? Most of us would rather not look too closely at our own blind spots. It's so much easier to point out what other people are doing wrong, to keep the story simple, and the blame safely out of reach.
But real change? That only happens when we're willing to see ourselves honestly—even if it stings a little.
Imagine a project leader, frustrated because their team just isn’t enthusiastic. For weeks, they’ve pushed harder, fired off more reminders, and grown more impatient. One night, after yet another tense exchange, the leader sits alone, replaying the day in their mind. Then a thought pops up: “Maybe I’m not as open as I think. Maybe my team feels shut down by me.”
Ouch, right? That’s uncomfortable—but it’s also a turning point.
Most of us avoid those moments. Our minds jump in to protect us, to explain away our mistakes, to insist, “Hey, the real problem is out there, not in here.” But when we find the courage to look inward, even for a second, something starts to shift. The stories we tell ourselves, the ones that felt so certain, suddenly don’t seem quite so solid.
That same leader, now aware of their own defensiveness, starts to approach their team in a whole new way. They ask for feedback. They listen—really listen—without cutting people off. And when they don’t have all the answers, they say so.
This kind of honesty isn’t easy. It takes humility—the willingness to admit you don’t see everything, that your point of view is limited, and yes, that you might be wrong. It also takes courage, because it means giving up the comfort that comes from blaming others.
But here’s the thing: the rewards are real. When we face our own self-deception, we become more open, more flexible, and a lot more compassionate. Relationships deepen, trust grows, and new possibilities start to show up. That leader who once felt all alone now finds support and real collaboration. The team, noticing the change, responds with a burst of new energy.
Most people don’t realize just how much energy goes into keeping up self-deception. All that justifying, defending, proving ourselves right—it’s exhausting. But when that weight finally lifts, there’s this incredible sense of relief. Almost like freedom. Suddenly, the world feels bigger, and the way forward is a whole lot clearer.
And it’s not about being perfect or never making mistakes. It’s about being willing to see, to learn, and to grow. Every time you choose honesty over self-justification, you’re taking a step out of the box—and you’re inviting others to do the same.
